name: Lake Titicaca & Puno
tagline: The world's highest navigable lake, home to a floating village built entirely from reeds and traditions still lived, not performed.
highlight: Stepping onto a Uros floating island for the first time, the spongy reed ground shifting slightly underfoot, unlike anywhere else on Earth.
shortDescription: The world's highest navigable lake, home to the Uros people's floating reed islands and the traditional weaving villages of Taquile and Amantaní.
metaDescription: A Lake Titicaca and Puno travel guide: the Uros floating islands, Taquile, Sillustani, food and how to plan a visit to Peru's high-altitude lake.
nearestAirport: Inca Manco Cápac International Airport (JUL), near Juliaca
knownFor: The Uros floating islands, Taquile weaving, high-altitude scenery
goodFor: Living culture, island life, high-altitude scenery

image.alt: The floating reed islands of the Uros people on Lake Titicaca

intro: Lake Titicaca is the world's highest navigable lake, a vast, deep-blue expanse straddling the Peru-Bolivia border at over 3,800 metres, ringed by traditional Andean communities.

Its most famous residents, the Uros people, live on floating islands built and continuously rebuilt from layers of totora reed, a way of life dating back centuries and still practised today, not staged for visitors.
Most visitors base themselves in Puno, a workaday lakeside city, using it to reach the Uros islands, Taquile's traditional weaving communities and the pre-Inca burial towers at nearby Sillustani.

whyVisit.intro: Lake Titicaca's case rests on living Andean culture found nowhere else on Earth, set against extraordinary high-altitude scenery.

points.title: The Uros floating islands are still inhabited
points.text: A real, ongoing way of life on islands rebuilt from reeds, not a recreation for tourists.

points.title: It's the world's highest navigable lake
points.text: A vast, deep-blue expanse at over 3,800 metres, striking simply for its scale.

points.title: Taquile Island's weaving is UNESCO-recognised
points.text: A textile tradition significant enough to be named Intangible Cultural Heritage.

points.title: Sillustani's burial towers are a serious archaeological site
points.text: Pre-Inca funerary towers on a peninsula overlooking a smaller neighbouring lake.

points.title: It offers a different side of Peru from Cusco
points.text: A quieter, more contemplative pace than the busier Machu Picchu circuit.

attractionsIntro: The region's essential sights combine living island communities with serious pre-Inca archaeology.

attractions.name: The Uros floating islands

image.file: File:Islas flotantes de los Uros, Lago Titicaca, Perú, 2015-08-01, DD 25.JPG
image.alt: The floating reed islands of the Uros people

attractions.text: Built entirely from layers of totora reed, continuously maintained as older layers rot away from below.
attractions.tip: A short boat ride from Puno's harbour, easily combined with Taquile in a single day trip.

attractions.name: Taquile Island
attractions.text: Home to a UNESCO-recognised weaving tradition, where men and women both knit and weave using techniques passed down for generations.
attractions.tip: An overnight homestay here offers a far deeper experience than a rushed day visit.

attractions.name: Amantaní Island
attractions.text: A quieter, less-visited island than Taquile, known for its two hilltop temples and warm homestay tradition.
attractions.tip: The climb to the island's temples rewards sweeping views over the lake at sunset.

attractions.name: Puno's Plaza de Armas

image.alt: Puno's Plaza de Armas and cathedral

attractions.text: The heart of Puno, a colonial square anchored by a baroque cathedral overlooking the city.
attractions.tip: A good spot to acclimatise gently before heading out onto the lake.

attractions.name: Sillustani

image.alt: The pre-Inca burial towers at Sillustani

attractions.text: Striking pre-Inca funerary towers, called chullpas, standing on a peninsula overlooking a smaller neighbouring lake.
attractions.tip: Visit in the late afternoon for the best light on the towers' stonework.

attractions.name: Lake Titicaca

image.file: File:Vista del Lago Titicaca en Perú.jpg
image.alt: The vast expanse of Lake Titicaca

attractions.text: The world's highest navigable lake, its scale and deep blue colour striking from nearly any vantage point.
attractions.tip: The light on the water changes dramatically through the day — worth seeing at more than one time.

attractions.name: Puno's waterfront

image.file: File:Vista de Puno y el Titicaca, Perú, 2015-08-01, DD 53-54 PAN.JPG

attractions.text: The departure point for nearly every lake excursion, a working harbour with sweeping views over the water.
attractions.tip: Arrive early for boat departures — the harbour gets busy with day-trip groups.

thingsToDoIntro: The region rewards slowing down, whether on a boat, an island homestay, or exploring Puno itself.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Uros floating islands

image.file: File:Islas flotantes de los Uros, Lago Titicaca, Perú, 2015-08-01, DD 44-48 PAN.jpg

thingsToDo.text: An essential half-day, meeting Uros families and learning how the islands are continuously rebuilt from reeds.
thingsToDo.tip: A small tip or purchase of local crafts is a welcome way to support the community you're visiting.

thingsToDo.title: Stay overnight on Taquile or Amantaní

image.alt: The view of Taquile Island from Amantaní

thingsToDo.text: A rewarding homestay experience, sharing a simple meal with a local family far from the day-trip crowds.
thingsToDo.tip: Pack a warm layer — island nights get cold even when days are mild.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Sillustani's burial towers

image.alt: Exploring the burial towers at Sillustani

thingsToDo.text: A worthwhile half-day trip from Puno, examining pre-Inca funerary architecture up close.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with a stop at a local llama and alpaca farm, common on organised tours here.

thingsToDo.title: Watch sunset from Amantaní

image.alt: Sunset over Lake Titicaca from Amantaní Island

thingsToDo.text: A memorable evening, watching the light fade over the lake from one of the island's hilltop temples.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring a proper jacket — temperatures drop sharply once the sun goes down.

thingsToDo.title: Wander Puno's Plaza de Armas
thingsToDo.text: A gentle way to spend a first afternoon, adjusting to the altitude before heading out on the lake.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with a coffee stop overlooking the square.

thingsToDo.title: Learn Taquile's weaving traditions
thingsToDo.text: A fascinating cultural experience, watching textiles produced using techniques recognised by UNESCO.
thingsToDo.tip: Handwoven textiles bought directly from Taquile's weavers make an especially meaningful souvenir.

foodIntro: Food here leans on fresh lake trout and hearty Andean staples suited to the high altitude.

foods.name: Trucha (Titicaca trout)
foods.text: The lake's signature dish, fresh trout served grilled or fried, often with quinoa or potatoes.
foods.whereToTry: Restaurants throughout Puno and on the lake's islands.

foods.name: Quinoa soup
foods.text: A warming Andean staple, hearty quinoa soup well suited to Puno's cold evenings.

foods.name: Cuy (guinea pig)
foods.text: A traditional Andean delicacy, found on menus throughout the wider Puno region.

foods.name: Lomo saltado

image.alt: Lomo saltado, a Peruvian stir-fry of beef, onions and fries

foods.text: A reliable classic, found on menus throughout Puno even at this altitude and distance from the coast.

foods.name: Coca tea
foods.text: Essential at this altitude, a mild herbal tea served at nearly every hotel and café in Puno.

foods.name: Pisco sour

image.alt: A pisco sour, Peru's national cocktail

foods.text: Available throughout Puno, though best enjoyed in moderation given the altitude.
foods.whereToTry: Bars and restaurants throughout the city.

accommodation.intro: Puno serves as the region's main base, with island homestays a rewarding alternative for a night or two.

areas.name: Puno city centre

areas.name: Taquile or Amantaní homestays

gettingThere.intro: Puno is reached by bus or flight via nearby Juliaca, with Cusco the most common connecting point.

options.mode: Overnight or day bus from Cusco
options.text: Comfortable on reclining-seat services, taking around six to seven hours.
options.detail: Some routes stop at scenic and historic sites along the way.

options.text: The fastest option, with a short onward drive of about 45 minutes to Puno.
options.detail: Connects to Lima and Cusco with regular daily flights.

options.text: A practical link for combining Titicaca with southern Peru.
options.detail: The scenic train route is a memorable, if slower, alternative to the bus.

gettingAround.intro: Boats are essential for reaching the lake's islands, with Puno itself easily walkable.

options.text: The standard way to reach the Uros islands, Taquile and Amantaní.
options.detail: Widely available from Puno's harbour, bookable a day or more ahead.

options.text: Easy — the city centre is compact and walkable, altitude permitting.
options.detail: Take it slowly given Puno's elevation, even higher than Cusco.

options.text: Useful for reaching sites outside the city, such as Sillustani.
options.detail: Organised tours are also widely available for this route.

bestTime.headline: May to September for the dry season, though the lake is visitable year-round
bestTime.summary: Puno's high altitude means it stays cool year-round, with the dry season offering the clearest lake views.

seasons.text: The clearest skies and most reliable boat conditions, though nights turn cold.
Fewer crowds with still-decent weather odds.
Warmer nights, though afternoon rain and choppier lake conditions are more common.

bestTime.avoid: Arriving without prior altitude acclimatisation — Puno sits even higher than Cusco, at around 3,800 metres.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make a Lake Titicaca and Puno visit noticeably smoother.
tips: Acclimatise in Cusco or elsewhere before arriving — Puno sits even higher, at around 3,800 metres.
Book boat tours a day ahead through your hotel or a local agency.
Pack warm layers regardless of season — lake nights turn cold year-round.
Consider an island homestay for a deeper, less rushed cultural experience.
Bring small cash for craft purchases on the Uros islands and Taquile.
Drink plenty of water and coca tea to help manage the high altitude.

faq.q: How many days do you need at Lake Titicaca?
faq.a: Two to three days covers the Uros islands, Taquile and Sillustani comfortably.

faq.q: Are the Uros floating islands still inhabited?
faq.a: Yes — around 1,200 Uros people still live on and maintain the islands, a real, ongoing way of life, not a recreation.

faq.q: Is Puno's altitude higher than Cusco's?
faq.a: Yes — Puno sits at around 3,800 metres, noticeably higher than Cusco's 3,400 metres, so prior acclimatisation helps.

faq.q: What is Lake Titicaca known for?
faq.a: Being the world's highest navigable lake, home to the Uros floating islands and traditional weaving communities on Taquile.

faq.q: Can you visit Lake Titicaca as a day trip?
faq.a: The Uros islands work as a half-day trip from Puno, though an overnight island homestay offers a far richer experience.

faq.q: How do you get from Cusco to Lake Titicaca?
faq.a: By overnight bus (around six to seven hours) or a short flight to nearby Juliaca, both common and comfortable options.
